The White-banded tyrannulet (Mecocerculus stictopterus) is a small Neotropical flycatcher inhabiting montane cloud forests where it gleans arthropods from foliage. Field studies in the Peruvian Andes indicate that newly hatched nestlings emerge from eggs incubated at 34 °C [T = 34 °C], and the age at hatching is approximately 14 days [ab = approximately 14 days]. At this critical developmental juncture, the chick weighs roughly 1.2 grams [Ww0 = roughly 1.2 grams], a modest initial mass typical of altricial passerine neonates that rely heavily on biparenal provisioning. This hatchling weight lays the foundation for a rapid growth trajectory toward adult body size, particularly among females, which achieve a substantially larger ultimate mass. The brood size and reproductive frequency of this species have been documented through long-term nest monitoring.

When held under thermal conditions corresponding to the species' typical active metabolic state at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], the maximum reproductive rate was reconstructed from two key demographic parameters. Breeding females typically lay 2 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 eggs per clutch] and produce approximately 1 clutch per year [F_R_i = approximately 1 clutch per year], yielding a modest annual fecundity that aligns with the slow-paced life history of many tropical montane insectivores. This reproductive output is consistent with patterns observed in congeners that occupy similar high-elevation niches. The measured basal oxygen consumption of adult birds provides further insight into the energetic underpinnings of this constrained reproductive strategy.

Under the same thermal regime of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], resting metabolic rate in adults reaches a maximum of 44 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 44 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that reflects the elevated energetic demands of maintaining endothermy in a cool, high-altitude environment. This metabolic rate is relatively high for a passerine of this body size and likely constrains the energy available for both self-maintenance and offspring production. The combination of a modest clutch size and a low annual breeding frequency may thus represent an energetic trade-off necessitated by the costs of thermoregulation in a montane habitat where temperatures frequently drop below thermoneutrality.

Development proceeds rapidly after hatching under the favorable temperatures associated with parental brooding at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight and nest departure, occurs at 14 days after hatching [tx = 14 days after hatching], a relatively short nestling period for a tropical insectivore at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. Puberty, or the attainment of sexual maturity, follows considerably later at 42 days after hatching [tp = 42 days after hatching], a delay that reflects the time required to complete skeletal growth and acquire full foraging proficiency at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. The period between fledging and puberty is a critical phase during which juveniles must refine their insect-hunting skills while avoiding predation.

Long-term mark-recapture studies have elucidated the extended life history of this high-elevation flycatcher. The oldest documented individuals reach a maximum lifespan of approximately 6.8 years [am = approximately 6.8 years] when maintained under thermal conditions at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], an exceptional longevity for a passerine of its size, which typically spans only 2 to 4 years. Furthermore, the time since birth at first brood for females is about 0.95 years [tR = about 0.95 years] at 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], indicating that individuals typically defer their initial breeding attempt until their second calendar year. Adult females reach a maximum body mass of 9.4 grams [Wwi = 9.4 grams], with field-caught birds ranging between 8 and 11 grams, placing Mecocerculus stictopterus among the smaller-bodied members of its genus.
